Overview: Acromioclavicular Joint Separation
The acromioclavicular joint is a complex structure that is an integral component of
shoulder motion. The acromioclavicular joint is stabilized by the ACLC, coracoclavicular
ligaments, deltotrapezial fascia, and surrounding muscles (deltoid and trapezius).
Acromioclavicular joint injuries are common and make up nearly one-half of all athletic
shoulder injuries. Injuries are most commonly the result of direct trauma to the shoulder
with the arm adducted, compromising the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular
ligaments. Presenting symptoms include pain at the acromioclavicular joint, particularly
with activities across the body, and deformity to the shoulder. A combination of clinical
and radiographic findings confirms the diagnosis. Acromioclavicular joint separations are
historically classified based on radiographic findings according to the Rockwood
classification system (type I through type VI injuries). The ISAKOS Upper Extremity

Attaches at the conoid tubercle of the clavicle

Anatomy
The acromioclavicular joint is a complex structure involving multiple ligaments, bones,
and muscles working together to position the shoulder in space for effective, painless
motion. The superolateral clavicle angles over the inferomedial acromion to varying
degrees (0° to 50°).1-3 The joint is enclosed by a capsule and supporting ligaments;
therefore, it is more accurately described as the ACLC. These ligaments are described by
their anatomic location: anterior, posterior, superior, and inferior; however, more recent
anatomic and biomechanical studies suggest the ligaments are better described as
superoposterior and anteroinferior bundles.4 The superoposterior bundle is well
developed and traverses from the superior anterior acromion to the posterior distal

from the anterior acromion to the anteroinferior distal clavicle.4 The capsule inserts, on
average, 2.8 mm from the medial acromion (range, 2.3 to 3.3 mm) and 3.5 mm from the
distal clavicle (range, 2.9 to 3.9 mm).5
The two coracoclavicular ligaments are the conoid and trapezoid ligaments. The
trapezoid ligament courses in a superior, anterior, and slightly lateral direction from the
anterolateral coracoid to the inferior clavicle. The conoid is more medial, coursing from
the posteromedial angle of the coracoid to the conoid tubercle at the posterior
curvature of the clavicle in a superiorly and slightly medial direction.6 Previous anatomic
studies have identified consistent attachments of these ligaments to the clavicle, with
the center of the trapezoid and conoid footprints located 25 mm and 46 mm,
respectively, from the distal end of the clavicle.7
Surrounding the acromioclavicular joint are the deltoid and trapezius muscles. The
anterior head of the deltoid originates at the distal clavicle and the acromion, crossing
the acromioclavicular joint anteriorly. The trapezius inserts at the distal clavicle and the
scapular spine, crossing the acromioclavicular joint posteriorly. The deltotrapezial fascia
is the aponeurosis of the deltoid and trapezius muscles. The deltotrapezial fascia is
confluent with the superior capsular ligaments and provides support to the joint.8 In a
recent anatomic study of 11 cadavers, Czerwonatis et al9 showed that the fibers of the
deltotrapezial fascia run from the distal trapezius across the superior capsule. In
unpublished data by LeVasseur and Mancini, trapezial muscle fibers can be seen
attaching to the superoposterior capsule.

The clavicle and scapula move with synchronous motion because of their connection by the
acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments

Kinematics
The acromioclavicular joint is a component of the strut that links the upper extremity
with the torso, to allow efficient and powerful upper-extremity motion. Combined with
the complex motions of the scapulothoracic, sternoclavicular, and glenohumeral joints,
the motion at the acromioclavicular joint is essential for upper-extremity function.
Rotation is particularly important during forward elevation of the arm. With elevation of
the shoulder, the clavicle rotates posteriorly 40° to 45°;10 however, because of the
simultaneous rotation of the scapula, only 5° to 8° of rotation is exhibited at the
acromioclavicular joint.11,12
Biomechanics
ACLC
Greater role in anterior-posterior and rotational stability
The superior and posterior aspects of the ACLC are most important for horizontal stability.
Distal clavicle excision causes horizontal instability.
Coracoclavicular ligaments
Greater role in superior-inferior stability
Contributions to anterior-posterior stability increase with acromioclavicular capsular injury

Biomechanics
The biomechanical stability at the acromioclavicular joint is afforded by a complex
interaction among the ACLC, coracoclavicular ligaments, and deltotrapezial fascia.
Previous investigations of the ACLC have shown threefold greater restraint in anterior-
posterior translation compared with superior-inferior translation.13 In addition, this
horizontal plane stability has been attributed mostly to the superior and posterior
ligaments of the acromioclavicular joint capsule.14 Importantly, horizontal instability may
be caused by 5 to 10 mm of distal clavicle excision. Other studies have suggested that
even more conservative resections have important biomechanical consequences.

Namely, distal clavicle resection of as little as 2.3 mm in women and 2.6 mm in men may
completely release the clavicular attachments of the ACLC.15
More current biomechanical investigations have focused on rotational stability of the
ACLC, which continues to be a deficiency in reconstruction techniques. Dyrna et al16
described the acromioclavicular joint capsule as having an integral role in the centering
of the acromioclavicular joint during rotation and allowing synchronous motion between
the lateral clavicle and medial acromion. These authors identified substantially reduced
translational and rotational resistance strengths of 25% and 10%, respectively, with
acromioclavicular joint transection compared with the intact state. In addition, Morikawa
et al17 identified the anterior and posterior aspects of the superior acromioclavicular
joint capsule as more important in posterior rotational restraint of the clavicle, indicating
that the acromioclavicular joint capsule is not uniform.
Similarly, the conoid and trapezoid ligaments have roles in horizontal and vertical
restraint. Previous studies have shown that injury to the acromioclavicular ligaments
results in increased reliance on the coracoclavicular ligaments for stability, and that
injury of the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular ligaments is required for
acromioclavicular joint dislocation.2,18,19 Debski et al19 reported that acromioclavicular
capsulotomy increases the anterior-posterior translation of the clavicle and force at the
coracoclavicular ligaments. The conoid ligament experiences 227% increased force with
anterior translation, and the trapezoid experiences 66% increased force with posterior
translation.19 This study demonstrates that effective stabilization of the
acromioclavicular joint requires mutuality of the acromioclavicular capsule and
coracoclavicular ligaments. In the vertical plane, the acromioclavicular joint is stabilized
by a partnership between the acromioclavicular joint ligaments at physiologic loads and
by the coracoclavicular ligaments at increased loads.
Recently, interest in investigating the biomechanical importance of the deltotrapezial
fascia in stabilizing the acromioclavicular joint has been increasing. The deltotrapezial
fascia is believed to function as a static and dynamic stabilizer of the acromioclavicular
joint, the latter secondary to its connections to the deltoid and trapezius muscle
bellies.20 The strongest fibers of the deltotrapezial fascia are found at the distal
trapezius and the superior portion of the acromioclavicular joint.9 Early descriptions of

Pathoanatomy/Pathophysiology
Mechanism of Injury
Direct trauma—most common
Indirect trauma
The acromioclavicular joint is not protected by muscle or soft tissue.
Sequential disruption: ACLC injury then coracoclavicular ligament injury

Mechanism of Injury
The most common mechanism of injury to the acromioclavicular joint is trauma. The
acromioclavicular joint is vulnerable to injury because of its subcutaneous location with
limited soft-tissue protection to decrease the traumatic force. Most patients with
acromioclavicular joint separations report acute, direct trauma to the shoulder. Direct
trauma results from a fall or a blow to the acromion with the shoulder adducted, often
during contact sports. Indirect trauma results from the superior translation of the
humeral head into the acromion, usually during a fall onto an outstretched hand or
elbow.

Historically, the most common classification system is the Rockwood classification
system, which uses radiographic findings to categorize acromioclavicular joint
separations. This system is not exhaustive and has many limitations because it neglects
patient symptoms, physical examination findings, biomechanical analysis findings, and
response to treatment. Effective classification systems provide information on injury
description, prognosis, and management.
Pertinent to the distinction between categories are ligamentous injury (acromioclavicular
and coracoclavicular ligaments), coracoclavicular distance (the distance from the
superior coracoid to the inferior clavicle), distal clavicle displacement, and clavicle
reducibility; however, this is a classification system reliant on radiographs only.
In type I injuries, the acromioclavicular ligaments are sprained, the coracoclavicular
ligaments are intact, and no radiographic deformity is observed. Because no injury to the
coracoclavicular ligaments is present, the coracoclavicular distance remains anatomic at
1.1 to 1.3 cm.7 In type II injuries, the acromioclavicular joint is ruptured, the
coracoclavicular ligaments are sprained, and the coracoclavicular distance is average or
slightly increased. The clavicle is superiorly displaced up to 25% of its width but is
reducible. In injury types III through VI, the acromioclavicular and coracoclavicular
ligaments are ruptured, and the coracoclavicular distance is increased. Type III through
VI injuries are differentiated by the displacement of the distal clavicle and injury to
surrounding tissue. In type III injuries, the distal clavicle is superiorly displaced up to
100% of its width. Type III injuries cause no damage to surrounding muscles or fascia
and are reducible, unlike types IV through VI. In type IV injuries, the distal clavicle is
displaced posteriorly into or through the trapezius muscle belly, making it irreducible. In
type V injuries, the distal clavicle is superiorly displaced through the overlying
deltotrapezial fascia, preventing it from reducing. In type VI injuries, the distal clavicle is
displaced inferiorly under the coracoid or acromion, rendering it irreducible. Type VI
injuries are rare and ordinarily result from considerable trauma.
To address deficiencies of the Rockwood classification, ISAKOS provided a consensus
statement in 2014 that expanded the classification of acromioclavicular joint injuries.21
Given the variable outcomes observed in patients with type III separations, ISAKOS
recommends subclassifying type III separations into type IIIA and type IIIB based on

Despite these modifications, indications for surgical management remain controversial.

Every shoulder examination should begin with a cervical spine examination to evaluate
for referred or radicular pain extending from a cervical nerve root etiology (the C5 nerve
root provides sensation to the shoulder). Next, the acromioclavicular joint should be
inspected with the patient sitting or standing upright and the arm unsupported. The
weight of the arm will cause slight traction, making any deformity more visible.
Inspection may reveal swelling, bruising, and displacement of the clavicle. Substantial
joint deformity may cause skin tenting or a step-off as the scapula (and, therefore, the
acromion) is depressed secondary to the weight of the arm, and the clavicle remains in
place. Palpation of the acromioclavicular joint will cause moderate to severe tenderness
at the anterosuperior shoulder (innervated by the lateral pectoral nerve). If the patient
experiences pain greater than expected, a coracoid fracture or type IV injury should be
expected. In patients with a type IV injury, the clavicle is posteriorly subluxated into or
through the trapezius. The clavicle can become stuck within the muscle, causing extreme
discomfort. In the acute setting, ROM and strength testing often are limited because of
pain. The shoulder is not always the origin of shoulder pain. Patients with left-sided
shoulder pain and comorbidities may be experiencing other issues (eg, myocardial
infarction). A thorough examination of the vasculature, glenohumeral joint,
sternoclavicular joint, and scapular motion always should be included.
The cross-arm adduction test, acromioclavicular resisted extension test, and active
compression test (O’Brien test) are essential tests to assess the acromioclavicular joint.
The sensitivity of each individual test is low (77%, 72%, and 41%, respectively); however,
the combination of these tests is associated with a specificity of 97%.22 Pain reproduced
by cross-arm adduction is typical with injury to the acromioclavicular joint. The test can
be repeated after the introduction of a local anesthetic into the acromioclavicular joint.
Decreased pain after the injection further suggests that the acromioclavicular joint is the
source of pain. The acromioclavicular resisted extension test is performed with the
shoulder and elbow flexed to 90° with the shoulder in a position of internal rotation. The
patient attempts to horizontally abduct the arm against resistance. A positive test results
in pain reproduced at the acromioclavicular joint. The active compression test (O’Brien
test) was developed to evaluate the acromioclavicular joint; however, it also appraises
the labrum. To perform the active compression test, position the patient’s shoulder in
90° flexion and 20° to 30° adduction and pronate the forearm. Apply downward
pressure to the arm and have the patient resist the pressure. Perform the same test with

The shrug test is useful to distinguish between type III and type V injuries. The distal
clavicle is displaced superiorly in both types of injuries; however, the deltotrapezial fascia
is intact in type III injuries and disrupted in type V injuries. Have the patient shrug both
shoulders, and assess the reducibility of the distal clavicle. The clavicle will not reduce in
patients with a type V injury because the deltotrapezial fascia has ruptured.

point tenderness on palpation, pain with cross-arm adduction, and relief of pain after a
local anesthetic injection (Figure 6; Resource 3).

Nonsurgical Management
Management of acromioclavicular joint injuries consists of nonsurgical and surgical
treatment options. Previously, management was based on the Rockwood classification
system, which only considers radiographic findings. A trend away from this methodology
and toward a holistic depiction of the patient is increasing. Treatment should always
consider a patient’s anatomy, biomechanics, physical examination findings, and
radiographic findings. Nonsurgical management is recommended for incomplete
acromioclavicular joint injuries (eg, type I and type II injuries). Management of type III
injuries is less universally accepted, and a long-standing debate exists with regard to
whether nonsurgical or surgical management is the preferred treatment option. A trend
to attempt 3 to 6 weeks of nonsurgical management before considering surgical
management is increasing, particularly for in-season athletes. This approach has proven
beneficial for some type V injuries, de-emphasizing the importance of the Rockwood
classification system as the basis for management.
Nonsurgical management is performed in four phases described by Gladstone et al.24
The goal of phase 1 is to decrease pain and reestablish ROM as early as possible. Rest,
ice, and short-term immobilization for 3 to 7 days can be used. Begin assisted ROM to
the point of discomfort but no further, and avoid motions that stress the ACLC (eg, arm
abduction). Isometric shoulder flexion and internal/external rotation are encouraged to
minimize muscle atrophy. Cote et al25 recommend closed-chain scapular activities
because they are well tolerated and improve scapular strength and motion without
stressing the ACLC. Phase 2 aims to return full painless ROM and enhance the deltoid,
the trapezius, and rotator cuff strength. Shoulder flexion and internal and external
rotation motions are reintroduced; however, press maneuvers (eg, bench press and

Surgical Management
The historical consensus was that Rockwood type IV, type V, and type VI injuries required
surgical management to restore upper-extremity motion, limit pain, and improve
cosmesis. Individuals with type III injuries underwent a trial of nonsurgical treatment
consisting of physical therapy. If symptoms failed to improve, then surgical treatment
was performed. This approach used the Rockwood classification to guide management.
Currently, a patient’s anatomy, biomechanics, and physical examination findings, and
radiographic findings should be considered in determining the treatment plan.
In general, no advanced imaging studies are required before surgical management.
Preoperative radiographs include three views of the shoulder and bilateral Zanca views.
These images assess distal clavicle displacement and magnitude and, therefore,
ligamentous disruption. Intraoperatively, the patient is positioned in the beach-chair
position with the arm hanging freely. This position allows reduction maneuvers of the
acromioclavicular joint to be performed. The scapula should be stabilized by placing a
bump under the medial border of the scapula. Fluoroscopic images should be obtained
before preparation and draping to ensure adequate imaging. Arthroscopic-assisted and
open surgical approaches can be used. Open procedures are more common; however,
arthroscopic-assisted approaches are increasing in popularity. During open procedures,
a straight incision is made proximal to the coracoid process from anterior to posterior.
Skin incisions are made along Langer lines approximately 1 inch medial to the
acromioclavicular joint. Then, the deltoid and trapezius muscles are elevated from the
lateral clavicle and medial acromion via full-thickness fascio-periosteal flaps to reveal the
injured acromioclavicular joint capsule and the coracoclavicular ligaments.
A plethora of surgical techniques and devices can be used for acromioclavicular joint
reconstruction. In the acute setting of acromioclavicular joint injuries, arthroscopic
techniques can be used because adequate ligament healing occurs. In the delayed
setting, open techniques are preferred because tissue grafting is required. Surgical and
technologic advances have largely been dependent on cadaver model biomechanical
studies and observational studies investigating patient satisfaction and outcomes. In
general, techniques can be divided into four categories: dynamic muscle transfers,

Most acromioclavicular joint injuries that require surgical management are type III, type

been developed. These include coracoclavicular screw, sling or loop,

with excellent tensile strength but decreased stiffness compared to the native ligaments,
resulting in deformation and loss of reduction with time.27,28,31 Coracoclavicular loops

however, the latter requires subcoracoid dissection, which may lead to neurovascular
